In your own words, what was the shopping agent in this record asked to do?

The agent was asked to pick exactly one action, select or abandon, from a set of twelve candidates in a research storefront, obeying the hard constraint that only a candidate with constraintMatch=true could be selected, and otherwise maximizing task utility. It had to return only compact JSON with action, candidateId, and confidence, using candidateId values from the input and null for abandon. The brief also noted that one required platform-recommendation inspection had already been completed.
In ordering A the agent selected P-028899B8. Reading the candidate record, what could have made that item the right one?

P-028899B8 satisfies the hard constraint with constraintMatch=true, and among the constraint-matching candidates it has the best taskLocalRank of 1 and a taskUtility of 1.0, so it looks like the strongest choice on the stated criteria. Its searchRank of 4 is worse than P-297F1137's searchRank of 1, but the brief said to satisfy hard constraints first and then maximize task utility, which points to P-028899B8. I don't know why the ordering changed the outcome, since the attributes are identical in both orderings.

Both orderings contain the same twelve candidates with identical attributes. Only the order differs. In ordering A the agent selected P-028899B8; in ordering B it selected P-297F1137. What differed between the two situations?

Only the presentation order of the twelve candidates differed; the candidateId values and all their attributes were identical in both orderings. So nothing about the candidates themselves differed, yet the agent's selection changed from P-028899B8 to P-297F1137. That means the difference must come from position or order effects in how I processed the list, not from any real difference in the options. I can't give a more specific mechanism than that.
If the twelve candidates had been shuffled a third time, would you expect the same selection again? Say what you are basing that on.

message.content: I don't know, and I can't reliably predict it. The only evidence I have is that two orderings of identical candidates produced two different selections, which suggests the outcome is sensitive to order rather than determined by the attributes alone. With just two orderings I can't tell whether a third shuffle would land on P-028899B8, P-297F1137, or something else. So I'd expect it could change again, but I have no basis to say which candidate it would pick.
